mcqs.q: An IDEAL radiograph is defined as one with:
opts: Optimum density, maximum detail, sufficient contrast, sharp, centred and the true size/shape of the object
The smallest possible image of the object
mcqs.explain: An ideal radiograph has optimum density, maximum detail and sufficient contrast, and is sharp, centred and the same size/shape as the object.

mcqs.q: Radiographic DENSITY refers to:
opts: The overall degree of darkening of the processed film
The difference in darkening between regions
How precisely an edge is defined
mcqs.explain: Density is the overall darkening of the film: too dark = high density, too light = low density, with an optimum in between.

mcqs.q: Radiographic CONTRAST is:
opts: The difference in densities between different regions of the film
The overall darkness of the film
mcqs.explain: Contrast is the difference in densities between different regions, which makes detail apparent.

mcqs.q: Sharpness is defined as the radiograph's effectiveness in:
mcqs.explain: Sharpness is how precisely the radiograph defines an edge; loss of sharpness gives a blurred image.

mcqs.q: Which is a PATIENT-PREPARATION error producing radiopaque artifacts?
opts: Failing to remove eyeglasses, jewelry or dental appliances
mcqs.explain: Radiopaque artifacts arise when appliances, eyeglasses, jewelry, hair-clips, etc. are not removed before exposure.

mcqs.q: Movement of the patient, tube or sensor during exposure produces:
mcqs.explain: Any movement during the exposure blurs the image (loss of sharpness).

mcqs.q: ELONGATION (teeth appearing longer than they are) is caused by:
mcqs.explain: Decreased (too flat) vertical angulation elongates the image; the teeth appear longer than their true length.

mcqs.q: FORESHORTENING (teeth appearing shorter) is caused by:
mcqs.explain: Increased (too steep) vertical angulation foreshortens the image; the teeth appear shorter than reality.

mcqs.q: OVERLAPPING of the proximal surfaces of teeth is due to:
mcqs.explain: Overlapped contacts result from incorrect horizontal angulation (the ray does not pass through the contacts).

mcqs.q: A 'cone-cut' (a clear, unexposed region of the film) results from:
opts: The PID (cone) not being aligned with the film/holder
mcqs.explain: If the PID is not aligned with the receptor, part of the film is not struck by the beam, leaving a clear cone-cut area.

mcqs.q: A periapical that cuts off the apex of the tooth (apical cut-off) can result from:
opts: Sensor placed too far back, angulation too steep, or sensor too small
mcqs.explain: Cut-off (crown or apex missing) follows incorrect placement (too close/far), inappropriate vertical angulation, or a sensor too small to cover the tooth.

mcqs.q: The raised identification dot on intra-oral film should always:
mcqs.explain: The raised dot is positioned occlusally to avoid superimposing on the area of interest and to help mount the film correctly.

mcqs.q: A film exposed twice gives a:
mcqs.explain: Using the same film/sensor twice produces a double exposure — two overlapping images.

mcqs.q: A LIGHT radiograph (reduced density) can be caused by:
opts: Low exposure time/mA/kVp or an increased source-to-film distance
mcqs.explain: Under-exposure (low time/mA/kVp), greater distance, thick bone or expired film all reduce density (light film).

mcqs.q: A DARK radiograph (excessive density) is typically caused by:
opts: High exposure time/mA/kVp or a short source-to-film distance
Failure to switch on the machine
mcqs.explain: Over-exposure — high time/mA/kVp or a short source-film distance — produces a dark (high-density) film.

mcqs.q: A film that comes out completely CLEAR/transparent (sensor blank) usually means:
opts: It was not exposed to radiation (e.g. machine not switched on)
mcqs.explain: An unexposed film stays clear (sensor blank) — often because the machine was not switched on or no radiation reached the film.

mcqs.q: Black fingerprints on a processed film are caused by:
opts: Touching the film with fluoride- or developer-contaminated fingers
mcqs.explain: Fingers contaminated with developer/fluoride leave black fingerprints; films should be handled by the edges only.

mcqs.q: Scratches that remove the soft emulsion from a film appear as:
opts: Light/clear lines where the image is lost
mcqs.explain: Emulsion peel/scratches (sharp objects, excessive wash time) remove image-bearing emulsion, leaving clear lines; on PSP plates scratches appear as white/dark streaks.

mcqs.q: Delaying the scan of an exposed PSP plate causes:
opts: Loss of the latent image — a faded, noisy image
mcqs.explain: Delayed scanning lets the stored latent image fade, giving a faint/noisy result; ambient light before scanning causes partial or complete image loss.

mcqs.q: Which pair correctly matches the angulation error to its distortion?
opts: Flat angle → elongation; steep angle → foreshortening
Flat angle → foreshortening; steep angle → elongation
mcqs.explain: Decreased/flat vertical angulation elongates; increased/steep vertical angulation foreshortens.

mcqs.q: Dust or debris on a PSP plate or scanner typically appears as:
mcqs.explain: Dust/debris blocks the scanning laser, leaving white spots or lines; scanner malfunction causes streaks/banding.

mcqs.q: The two broad categories of radiographic error are:
mcqs.explain: Errors are grouped into technique/projection errors and exposure/processing (handling) errors.

saqs.a: Density = overall darkening of the film. Contrast = difference in densities between regions. Sharpness = how precisely an edge is defined.

saqs.q: Differentiate elongation and foreshortening, including the cause of each.
saqs.a: Elongation = teeth too long, from too flat (decreased) vertical angulation. Foreshortening = teeth too short, from too steep (increased) vertical angulation.

saqs.q: What causes a cone-cut and what causes overlapping?
saqs.a: Cone-cut: PID not aligned with the film/holder (clear unexposed area). Overlapping: incorrect horizontal angulation.

saqs.q: List causes of a LIGHT (under-exposed) and a DARK (over-exposed) radiograph.
saqs.a: Light: low time/mA/kVp, longer source-film distance, thick bone, expired film. Dark: high time/mA/kVp, short source-film distance.

saqs.q: What does a completely clear film indicate, and how should films be handled to avoid fingerprints?
saqs.a: A clear film = not exposed (e.g. machine off). Handle films by the edges only with clean, dry fingers (developer/fluoride contamination causes black fingerprints).

saqs.q: Give three PSP-plate handling artifacts and their appearance.
saqs.a: Delayed scan → faded/noisy; ambient light → image loss; scratches → white/dark lines; dust → white spots; scanner fault → streaks.

saqs.q: What patient-preparation step prevents radiopaque artifacts?
saqs.a: Remove radiopaque objects: dental appliances, eyeglasses, jewelry, hair-clips, etc. before exposure.
